articles.title_orig: Investigation of alleged gang-rape at Cornell University fraternity house reopened
articles.title_zh: Investigation of alleged gang-rape at Cornell University fraternity house reopened
articles.content_orig:
Outrage over treatment of alleged offenders, members of Chi Phi fraternity, has grown since lawsuit was made public
Sign up for the Breaking News US newsletter email
Prosecutors in New York said on Monday that they have reopened an investigation into the alleged gang-rape of a student at Cornell University after an outcry over “leniency” shown to seven fraternity members named as the perpetrators.
According to lawyers for the student, who filed a civil lawsuit against the university and her alleged attackers earlier in September, only two members of the Chi Phi fraternity were expelled after the October 2024 incident, in which she said she was drugged and repeatedly raped over the course of seven hours.
None of the seven were arrested, they said, and the others were made to write essays, attend workshops or serve short suspensions.
On Monday, Matthew Van Houten, the Tompkins county district attorney, said his office was looking again at the case, after the woman, who was 20 at the time of the alleged assault, presented allegations in her lawsuit that were “dramatically different” from the statement she gave to police two years ago.
“It’s our intention to present the case to the Tompkins county grand jury with Jane Doe’s cooperation,” Van Houten told ABC News , using the name from the lawsuit to identify the woman.
“We want to re-examine whether there’s additional evidence that we were not aware of in November of 2024, that exists now that would change our assessment of the case and would result in the grand jury finding that there was criminal conduct.”
Outrage over the treatment of the alleged offenders has grown since the lawsuit was made public. The woman, who quit the university afterwards, said she went to visit a friend at the Chi Phi frat house in an already intoxicated state – and was made to snort a drug they told her was ketamine.
While they sexually assaulted her, she alleges, a message was sent to a frat house Snapchat group called Chi Phi Actives that stated there was “free pussy upstairs”.
At least five other frat members showed up and joined in, she said, and her ordeal lasted until about 5.45am. She made a report to campus police about three weeks later.
Cornell’s vice-president for university relations, Kyle Kimball, issued a statement on 21 September calling the allegations “deeply disturbing”. Kimball’s statement claimed the Ivy League institution’s offices of civil rights, student conduct and community standards carried out a number of inquiries at the time.
“The Xi chapter of Chi Phi fraternity remains barred from our campus,” Kimball’s statement also said. “Federal privacy law prohibits Cornell from disclosing specific information regarding individual students and we therefore are unable to make a public statement on any other disciplinary response.
“Violations of university policies could lead to sanctions up to and including suspension or expulsion. We will respond in detail through the legal process.”
An attorney for the student told CBS News that none of the alleged perpetrators faced legal consequences for their conduct, and nobody in the frat house that saw the message did anything to stop the rapes from taking place.
“Not one of these guys was arrested,” said the lawyer, Thomas Giuffra. “Not one. That I can tell you for a fact.
“There were so many people that could have prevented it and they didn’t. I’ve never seen anything like it.”
Giuffra also countered the statement of Van Houten, the Tompkins district attorney, which lays out what he said the alleged victim stated in her original police complaint from November 2024.
“She never says that she was drugged without her knowledge,” Van Houten said.
“She admits to taking drugs and alcohol voluntarily and with knowledge. She does not allege that she was forced to engage in any acts. She does not say that she was physically helpless or unconscious or incapacitated at any point during the time at the fraternity house.”
Giuffra told ABC News that neither the district attorney or Cornell police ever followed up with his client.
“In my experience, speaking with an abuse survivor requires delicacy, understanding and specialized training,” he said.
“An average university police officer would not have these skills. It would be the role of a specially trained detective or district attorney. However, Ms Doe was never contacted by anybody with those skills.”
Named defendants in the lawsuit are Matthew Ingalls, Johnathan Newell, Winston Lee, Gillio Lopes, Diego Sarabia, Scott Norris and Scott Kretzschmar.
Two of those defendants denied the allegations in statements to ABC News .
“At bottom, Scott never sexually assaulted or even touched the plaintiff in any way,” Jeremy Saland, an attorney for Kretzschmar, said. “Period.”
Norris denied engaging in sexual activity or drug use – but acknowledged he sent a message that was included in the complaint.
“I thoughtlessly engaged in Snapchat and briefly stopped in the room where misconduct happened but not when it happened,” he said.
On Sunday, the Academy Award-nominated actor Florence Pugh posted a lengthy statement on Instagram about Giuffra’s client, praising the “unbelievably powerful” victim and her “strong will”.
“This is really the moment where we need our men to be as horrified and as sickened as us,” Pugh wrote. “You need to be leading conversations about how we change the allowance and complicity of this behaviour as much as we are.”
Information and support for anyone affected by rape or sexual abuse issues is available from the following organizations. In the US, Rainn offers support on 800-656-4673. In the UK, Rape Crisis offers support on 0808 500 2222. In Australia, support is available at 1800Respect (1800 737 732). Other international helplines can be found at ibiblio.org/rcip/internl.html

articles.title_orig: SpaceX's Starship rocket orbiting Earth for first time after Texas lift-off - watch live
articles.title_zh: SpaceX's Starship rocket orbiting Earth for first time after Texas lift-off - watch live
articles.content_orig:
The largest rocket developed by SpaceX has successfully reached orbit, marking an important milestone for the private aerospace company.
“Starship is orbital,” mission control announced to cheers on a livestream on Monday that showed the spacecraft’s launch from a base in Texas in the United States.
The uncrewed spacecraft almost didn’t achieve the long-desired goal after one of its engines shut down too soon. But with everything else working well and the bad engine no longer needed, flight controllers decided after several tense minutes to proceed as planned.
Founder Elon Musk’s showpiece rocket – the biggest and most powerful ever built – carried 26 of the latest and most advanced Starlink satellites to join the 11,000 older models already providing internet service. It was Starship’s 14th full-scale launch from Texas’s southern tip in three years. The earlier test flights ventured no farther than the Indian Ocean halfway around the world, often crashing in flames and briefly skimming space.
This time, SpaceX was intent on circling the globe from an altitude of 275km (170 miles) – not just once but six times over almost 10 hours, ending with a Pacific splashdown near Chile. The first-stage booster wasn’t meant to return to the Starbase launch site, either, instead dropping into the Gulf of Mexico within minutes of the morning liftoff.
SpaceX wants to ensure that everything works before flying Starship back to Starbase. If the spacecraft breaks apart over land and rains debris onto people, “our popularity would diminish very rapidly”, Musk said at a business summit earlier this month. “That’s why we’re being extremely cautious here.”
If all goes well with this orbital debut, the next Starship will return to the launch pad with giant mechanical arms grabbing the hovering spacecraft. If the catch works – Musk gives it even or slightly better odds – then SpaceX will re-fly the spacecraft by year’s end or early next.
The 124 metre (407-foot) rocket was designed from the start to be fully reusable – a key to lowering launch costs. SpaceX managed to salvage the last Starship from the Indian Ocean in July. Engineers modified the newly launched Starship’s heat shield based on hands-on inspections from the recovered spacecraft, which is being tugged back to Starbase.
SpaceX is pressing hard to certify Starship for orbital flight, a vital step towards moon and Mars travel.
NASA’s Artemis III mission is coming up as soon as next summer, and will feature a triple-launch docking exercise in orbit around Earth between an Orion capsule full of astronauts and competing lunar landers. Jeff Bezos’s Blue Moon will blast off first, then Orion – which will close in for a linkup – then Musk’s Starship for a docking with Orion once Blue Moon launches.
The next mission – Artemis IV, slated for no sooner than 2028 – would have astronauts landing on the moon in either Blue Moon or Starship, whichever is ready first. Subsequent moonshots will alternate between the two billionaires’ landers.
Musk originally developed Starship for Mars, intending to launch scores of them with the red planet’s first settlers. For now, he plans to focus on the moon and use Starship to haul satellites into orbit by the truckload, phasing out the company’s frailer Falcon 9 rocket within several years. A second Starship launch site is nearing completion at Florida’s Kennedy Space Center and a third is planned for the US state of Louisiana.

articles.title_zh: Live updates: SpaceX launches unprecedented test flight of massive Starship, aiming for orbit
articles.content_orig:
• Liftoff successful: SpaceX’s Starship rocket, the most powerful rocket ever made, has launched from Starbase, Texas. The mission will seek to reach orbit for the first time during a 10-hour flight, deploying 26 operational Starlink satellites.
• What to expect: SpaceX will not attempt to land the Super Heavy rocket booster or return the upper Starship spacecraft to dry land. Both will aim for controlled splashdowns in the ocean.
• Coming up: SpaceX is facing intense pressure to get Starship ready for a crucial NASA test flight next year that could pave the way for the next moon landing.
You may have noticed that not all rocket-related headlines have been about the “ peaceful uses of outer space ” lately.
The United States recently revealed that it has deployed weapons into space for the first time, without saying what type of weapons or what they were intended to accomplish.
It’s only the latest in a long list of signs that space is rapidly becoming more militarized.
SpaceX has always played a massive role in supporting the United States’ strategic interests in orbit. The company famously once sued the US Air Force for the right to bid on rocket contracts ( and won ). The company now dominates the national security launch market.
And SpaceX’s space-based internet infrastructure has a national security bent of its own.
Starship’s task today was to deploy Starlink internet satellites that will help serve some of the company’s 12 million customers across 160 countries. But SpaceX is also using its space-based communications infrastructure to create a secure, military-grade network called Starshield for more than $6 billion.
Musk mentioned the secretive project during an August town hall, saying, “We can’t say too much about Starshield for obvious reasons — because it’s you know top secret and stuff — but the Starshield team has done amazing work, and it is now a vital part of America’s national security.”
The Department of War also recently announced it’s giving its workers access to Starshield AI’s Grok. (Grok, the AI model developed by xAI, is now part of SpaceX after a pre-IPO merger in February .)
Recent regulatory filings show that NASA administrator Jared Isaacman donated a whopping $3 million to President Donald Trump’s MAGA Inc. super Pac.
It’s a remarkably large donation and deeply unusual for a presidential appointee who is already confirmed to their post — espeicially a NASA appointee, as the space agency typically aims to position itself as apolitical.
NASA declined to comment on the donations, saying personal contributions fall outside the scope of the space agency’s communications duties. Isaacman told CNN that he has made “political and philanthropic donations” and declined to comment further on the matter.
Columbia law professor Richard Briffault, a campaign finance and government ethics expert, told CNN in an interview last week that there is nothing illegal about making such a donation — as unusual as it is. But it does raise ethics concerns, at least from an optics standpoint.
“It goes to the question of appearances: Is this an independent public servant serving the public interest, or is this somebody who is acting as a politician?” Briffault said.
This isn’t Isaacman’s first major donation to a Trump PAC. Last year, when Isaacman was attempting to get his nomination to lead NASA reinstated, he donated about $2 million to MAGA Inc. (Trump initially pulled the nomination, as CNN reported, because Isaacman had previously donated to Democrats. It was later reinstated, and Isaacman was confirmed in December.)
SpaceX CEO Elon Musk has a preexisting relationship with Isaacman, as the Isaacman has paid SpaceX to fly him on two missions to orbit. Isaacman has repeatedly said he would not favor SpaceX in his official capacity.
Musk has also closely aligned himself with Trump and donated millions to MAGA Inc. But recently, Musk also expressed some regret about taking such a substantial role in campaigns.
“I got too involved in politics,” he told The Economist during a recent interview.
SpaceX will not allow Starship to stay in orbit for 10 hours, as the company had originally planned.
Mission controllers, during a recent “checkpoint” analysis, decided to end the mission a bit early.
Huot noted that Starship was able to deploy all 26 of its Starlink satellites and the company has made contact with each of them, marking a huge mission success. But it won’t complete quite as many laps of the planet at originally hoped for.
NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman chimed in on social media to congratulate SpaceX on its success so far, getting the upper Starship spacecraft, or “ship,” to orbit for the first time.
All 26 of SpaceX’s new Starlink V3 satellies are currently in orbit.
SpaceX already confirmed contact with at least some of them. There’s no word yet on the status of the satellites that were designed to also snap pictures of Starship’s heat shield as they flew away from the vehicle.
SpaceX has put a massive emphasis on studying and improving Starship’s heat shield. It’s designed to protect the vehicle as it makes the grueling journey back home, as diving back into Earth’s thick atmosphere can involve temperatures topping 2,500 degrees Fahrenheit.
Starship is currently in orbit, but SpaceX previously decided that it would reevaluate the flight plan every so often to ensure that things are safe and looking good. One of those checkpoints is coming up.
“We’ll get to that initial checkpoint at about one hour 28 minutes into the flight . That’s where the team can look at everything and decide: Do we need to come home early?” SpaceX spokesperson Dan Huot said.
SpaceX can direct Starship to relight an engine and begin its trip home prematurely if anything goes wrong. That’s all designed to make sure Starship remains safe and does not lose control in orbit.
If SpaceX were to lose control of the vehicle as it is lapping the planet, it could remain stuck in orbit, posing a risk to active satellites.
SpaceX’s Starship conducted its 14th flight test on Monday, an unprecedented test flight to reach orbit.
Some of the 26 Starlink V3 satellites that Starship will deploy today are doing double duty: Before they go on to beam internet service to some of SpaceX’s 12 million internet customers, a few of these devices will play a role in researching how today’s test flight is going.
The heat shield is a vital component. It’s designed to protect the upper Starship spacecraft as it navigates the violent physics of reentering Earth’s thick inner atmosphere while traveling at speeds that can top 17,000 miles per hour.
And Starship’s heat shield doesn’t just have to work once. It has to work over and over and over again if SpaceX is going to realize its dream of rapidly reusing these rockets.
It’s perhaps one of the most daunting engineering challenges in a long list of technical quandaries that Starship is facing.
SpaceX confirmed it’s already made contact with the first Starlink V3 satellites after they were ejected from Starship’s cargo bay.
These are the first of a new generation of Starlinks that are intended to boost the network’s performance:
The Starship spacecraft has begun deploying its batch of 26 Starlink V3 satellites, the very first of a new generation of capacity-boosting Starlinks as SpaceX continues to build out its high-speed global internet business.
The Starlinks are designed to lie flat, stacked atop each other as they ride inside Starship’s cargo bay. They leave the vehicle by exiting through a narrow slat, sort of like a high-tech Pez dispenser.
One of Starship’s six engines just briefly reignited, as expected, and has officially sent the vehicle on a path to enter Earth orbit.
It’s a massive milestone. From here on out, Starship is traveling fast enough and at such a precise trajectory, that it’s begun falling around the planet.
Today’s test flight is expected to see Starship complete six full laps of Earth over about 10 hours.

articles.content_orig:
China has ‘wiretapped the Red Sea,’ ex-White House official warns as satellite images reveal new spy hub ahead of Xi visit.
Beijing has transformed the Red Sea into a dangerous surveillance hub, a former Pentagon official warned Sunday, after a new report revealed upgrades to China’s military footprint just six miles from a key $66 million-a-year U.S. military base in Djibouti, Africa.
The report by the Washington-based Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) cited new facilities which it said would likely enable the Chinese military to monitor activities of other militaries operating nearby, although it also clarified it was not possible to determine whether China was actively intercepting communications.
The developments, one defense expert told Fox News Digital, could also inject fresh tension into U.S.-China relations in the run-up to Chinese President Xi Jinping's visit to the White House on Sept. 24. Beijing's intelligence-gathering capabilities are already under renewed scrutiny.
"What China is clearly doing is building eavesdropping capabilities. That seems to be their aim," said Morgan Murphy , former Trump White House official and press secretary for Mark Esper when he was secretary of defense during the first Trump administration.
CHINA-LINKED SPY SITE EXPANSION IN CUBA RAISES ALARMS NEAR KEY US MILITARY BASES
Morgan Murphy said it was significant that China has chosen to place its only overseas base six miles from America's base in Djibouti. ( STR/AFP via Getty Images)
"Beijing has clearly wiretapped the Red Sea. When you build a 30-meter (100-foot-wide) satellite dish and cover it with a dome, so nobody can see where it's pointing, it's pretty clear you're up to no good," Murphy added while stating of the Washington-based think tank, that "the specificity here reflects the thorough research we expect out of CSIS."
The report pinpoints a large southeastern facility showing a control building, three 30-meter dipole antennas for high-frequency communications, two smaller antennas for very and "ultra-high frequencies," three mobile satellite dishes, four probable 5G towers and what CSIS said was a "radome" covering an unidentified asset.
CSIS also highlighted two new communications facilities that it says have emerged since 2024 that are likely to form part of a C4ISR command architecture, expanding China’s ability to intercept signals, track naval movements and communicate with Beijing while monitoring foreign militaries in the region.
The facilities would provide China with "a much more robust picture of the operating environment in the region," the report said.
CHINESE HACKERS TARGET NASA AND KEY US AGENCIES, DOJ ALLEGES
CSIS said commercial satellite imagery revealed that China’s military had installed new antennas, satellite communications equipment and signals intelligence assets at its base in Djibouti — its only formally acknowledged overseas military installation. (Planet Labs / Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS))
"This isn’t a supply depot — it’s a 50-yard line seat over America’s power projection and the U.S. Navy," Murphy said before stating that the U.S. has "128 bases in more than 51 countries — China has just one."
"But look at the location — a few miles from Camp Lemonnier, overlooking the choke point that moves roughly a sixth of global sea trade. Great powers don’t plant listening posts next to rival fleets for 'logistics,'" he warned.
"Britain held Gibraltar to see who entered the Med while Japan’s island radios came before the runways. The Soviets’ overseas sites were never just about fuel and Beijing is running that playbook on the Red Sea," Murphy added.
Although China’s Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jian said China is "unaware of the specific situation" and framed the country as a "builder of international peace," the new facilities provide Beijing with a picture of regional operations, according to Reuters.
CHINA IS BUILDING A MASSIVE SHIP THAT SHOULD SCARE AMERICANS ABOUT THE FUTURE
Beijing has transformed the Red Sea into a surveillance hub, former Pentagon officials warned after a new report revealed upgrades to China’s military footprint in Djibouti. ( DAPHNE BENOIT/AFP via Getty Images)
"The new report is helpful in framing the conversation, and it comes at an awkward time for China because Xi Jinping is visiting the White House on the 24th of this month," Murphy said.
"I'd bet a box of donuts this issue comes up. There is going to be public exposure of this, which Chinese leadership isn't used to. They aren't used to being asked tough questions by the press," he said.
President Donald Trump recently addressed Chinese intelligence efforts aboard Air Force One, acknowledging that China "spies on us" just as "we spy on them."
Trump's comments followed a report by The Wall Street Journal linking support from a Chinese entity to high-resolution satellite imagery used by Iran prior to a deadly missile attack on U.S. troops in Jordan.
"They basically do what we do," Trump noted, adding that "Xi has behaved reasonably well, and we behave reasonably well. ... You know what they say? That China spies on us. I say you're right, and we spy on them, too," he said, according to Reuters .
RUSSIA IS HELPING CHINA CLOSE GAP WITH US FORCES AMID TAIWAN TENSIONS, WARNS LONGTIME MILITARY LEADER
President Donald Trump greets Chinese President Xi Jinping ahead of a bilateral meeting at Gimhae Air Base on Oct. 30, 2025 in Busan, South Korea. Trump said he wants to keep the Strait of Hormuz open in the Middle East for countries, including China. (Andrew Harnik/Getty Images)
Murphy noted, "Nations spy on each other — allies and adversaries alike."
"It is a very old playbook, and listening posts all over the world are typical of great powers, but where the metal hits the floorboard is when you try to use that information," he said before adding that China may "keep tabs on us, but they cannot project power like the United States can."
The proximity of China's facility to U.S. operations is a core concern. Located less than six miles from Camp Lemonnier — the primary U.S. counterterrorism hub in Africa — and near French, Italian and Japanese installations, the site has a history of friction with U.S. forces.
"We are just right around the corner from China, and yet it's not a cooperative relationship," Murphy explained.
"Back in 2018, they lasered two of our C-130 pilots' eyes who suffered lasting damage from that incident. Beijing denied it, of course, but we know the truth."
WE SHOULD USE REAGAN AS A GUIDE IN HANDLING OUR MODERN ARMS RACE WITH CHINA
U.S. military aircraft as seen at Camp Lemonnier in Djibouti. Camp Lemonnier is the only permanent United States military base in Africa. (Getty Images)
During the 2018 incident , the Pentagon had formally complained to China after military-grade lasers were pointed at American pilots attempting to land at Camp Lemonnier, causing minor injuries.
While Beijing dismissed the allegations as "groundless accusations," the confrontation underscored the potential for friction between military forces operating from nearby bases.
"China has one overseas base. The United States has more than 128 — by some counts, over 700 installations around the world," Murphy said.
"So it's significant that China has chosen to place its only overseas base six miles from ours in Djibouti. It is hugely strategically important, which is why, of course, we're there."
IS TRUMP CONSIDERING BOLD AFRICA PLAY TO PUSH BACK ON CHINA, RUSSIA AND ISLAMIC TERRORISTS?
The northwest facility at the Chinese base in Djibouti features a possible communications building and a "radome" with an unidentified asset, images show. (Planet Labs / Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS))

articles.title_orig: Robert Pattinson’s Star Power and Gen Z: 5 Reasons ‘Primetime’ Became a Breakout Box Office Hit
articles.title_zh: Robert Pattinson’s Star Power and Gen Z: 5 Reasons ‘Primetime’ Became a Breakout Box Office Hit
articles.content_orig:
Senior Film and Media Reporter
Plenty of moviegoers had a seat for “ Primetime ,” a true-crime thriller starring Robert Pattinson as Dateline NBC journalist and “To Catch a Predator” host Chris Hansen.
The A24 movie landed on the higher end of box office expectations, scoring $19.2 million from 2,863 North American venues in its opening weekend. Although “Primetime” ranked in fourth place on domestic charts — behind Disney’s “Avengers: Endgame Encore” ($26 million), Sony’s “Resident Evil” reboot ($23 million) and fellow newcomer, Paramount’s wilderness adventure “The Heart of the Beast” ($20 million) — it cost just $15 million to produce and is already well-positioned to turn a profit theatrically.
Notably, “Primetime” marks the third-best opening weekend ever for A24, behind this summer’s sleeper hit “Backrooms” ($81.4 million) and Alex Garland’s 2024 dystopian “Civil War” ($25.5 million) and, impressively, above Josh Safdie and Timothée Chalamet’s 2025 ping-pong drama “Marty Supreme” ($15.7 million). This is Pattinson’s second consecutive hit with A24 following this spring’s dark relationship dramedy “The Drama,” which co-starred Zendaya and opened to $14.3 million domestically.
Directed by Lance Oppenheim, “Primetime” revolves around the production of “To Catch a Predator” and Hansen’s increasingly frenetic attempts to confront child sexual predators in complex sting operations. Critics embraced the movie, which holds an 87% on Rotten Tomatoes. Moviegoers gave “Primetime” a mixed “B” grade on CinemaScore exit polls, which isn’t all that surprising given the film’s intentionally unsettling nature.
“Considering the tough subject material, the audience score is good,” says David A. Gross, who publishes the box office newsletter FranchiseRe. “This is a hit.”
Here are five reasons “Primetime” was, well, ready for primetime at the box office.
It’s been a big year for Pattinson, the “Twilight” heartthrob-turned-bona-fide movie star. In 2026, he’s been in “The Drama,” Christopher Nolan’s summer smash “The Odyssey” and will appear in the upcoming sci-fi sequel “Dune: Part III.” While he shares the credit with Zendaya and Nolan for those wins, Pattinson is undeniably the draw in “Primetime.” More than 75% of audiences cited Pattinson as their No. 1 reason for buying a ticket, according to exit polls from PostTrak. What’s more impressive is Pattinson managed to get people to theaters without too splashy a press tour. (In addition to starring in just about every movie this year, he’s been busy filming “The Batman: Part II” in London.) He didn’t scale the Sphere in Las Vegas or advertise on blimps to get out the word about “Primetime.” Pattinson showed up at Venice Film Festival, where “Primetime” bowed to raves, and participated in some phone interviews . But otherwise, he let the movie do the talking.
Opening weekend crowds for “Primetime” skewed heavily Gen Z, with 69% of audiences under the age of 30. That’s especially significant because most Zoomers were way too young to watch “To Catch a Predator” when the show aired from 2004-2007. It helped that “Primetime” tapped into their love for the true-crime genre. This also highlights the audience that A24 has cultivated over the years, thanks to edgy, aesthetic and conversation-starting arthouse favorites like “Marty Supreme,” “Lady Bird,” “Everything Everywhere All at Once” and more. “Primetime” is the indie studio’s second release of the year to become a full-fledged event for younger moviegoers. The first was “Backrooms,” which became a wildly profitable breakout sensation with $400 million against a $10 million budget. It’s all a huge relief to theater owners, who worried that younger generations viewed the big screen as outdated.
Pattinson, meanwhile, might credit the win to Gen Z supporting their own. Pattinson has joked that he’s Gen Z (despite being 40, which makes him squarely a Millennial). During Vanity Fair’s Lie Detector test , his “Die My Love” co-star Jennifer Lawrence hilariously accused Pattinson of thinking he’s Gen Z because he likes to cold-call people on FaceTime. He claimed his birth year “doesn’t matter,” to which she replied, “I believe that you believe you’re Gen Z.”
A24 ran an effective social media-heavy campaign for “Primetime.” But whether he intended to or not, the real-life Hansen also stoked a ton of interest by continuously speaking out against the movie. Way before he got to see the film, Hansen was vocal in his criticism about Pattinson’s “overly dramatic” portrayal of him. He also stressed that “Primetime” isn’t a literal account of his career and questioned the studio’s “motive” in dramatizing the making of the hit reality series. When Hansen finally watched “Primetime,” he wasn’t all that enthused . He called the film “so bizarre” and “detached from reality.” In the process, he made plenty of headlines and put “Primetime” on the radar of “To Catch a Predator” fans across the country.
The Venice Film Festival can be hit or miss in terms of launching a movie into the mainstream. For every critical and commercial success like “A Star Is Born,” “The Shape of Water” and “La La Land,” there’s a high-profile misfire à la “Joker: Folie à Deux” or “After the Hunt.” Venice worked as the kickoff for “Primetime,” which was embraced with an enthusiastic seven-minute standing ovation . Since there weren’t many Hollywood-backed movies at the glamorous Italian festival, “Primetime” became the talk of Lido — leading to weeks of positive world-of-mouth before general audiences saw the film. That’s amore!
Oppenheim, the 30-year-old filmmaker known for documentaries like “Some Kind of Heaven” and HBO’s “Ren Faire,” was already emerging as a major emerging talent after “Primetime,” his narrative feature debut. And then, just days after “Primetime” launched at Venice, Oppenheim reached a new level of fame after he and comedian Nathan Fielder unveiled their top-secret documentary “You Can See Everything,” about Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes, at Telluride Film Festival . Seemingly overnight, Oppenheim found himself on everyone’s radar, which brought even more eyes to this project. Call it the Elizabeth Holmes bump?

articles.title_orig: White House releases new taxpayer-funded ad describing ‘final battle’
articles.title_zh: White House releases new taxpayer-funded ad describing ‘final battle’
articles.content_orig:
The Trump administration put out a new ad this weekend as part of its “PSA” campaign, this time showing President Donald Trump walking down a hallway as he asks people to join him in his fight to “expel the warmongers from our government.”
The ad — which at the end says it was “Paid for by the U.S. government” — is nearly identical to an ad put out by Trump’s 2024 presidential campaign.
Trump posted that ad to Truth Social in January 2024. The repurposed ad now includes “Paid for by the U.S. government.” But it excludes the last few seconds of the 2024 ad, which ends with text reading “Join President Trump’s fight to save America” and his 2024 campaign logo.
The ad signals an expansion of the White House’s controversial use of government funds to air pieces that resemble campaign advertisements. Last week, the White House ran a television ad in which Trump described how he wanted to “defeat communism,” set to the song “Love Me” by JMSN . The White House has called the ads “public service announcements.”
In the latest ad, dramatic black-and-white video shows President Trump walking down a hallway with audio of him saying it is the “final battle” and vowing to “demolish the deep state” and “throw off the sick political class that hates our country.”
“We will rout the fake news media, and we will liberate America from these villains once and for all,” it concludes.
Federal law requires political advertisers to submit certain public disclosures and generally bans using public funds for political advertising. Since the administration maintains the ads are public service announcements, it’s not clear whether those disclosures are available. The White House has not released a specific source of government funding used to air the ads.
AdImpact, a political ad tracking firm, has estimated that the administration has spent more than $1.7 million to run these ads, which have been running heavily in recent days during prominent television programming like football games, Sunday morning news shows, and prime time broadcast shows. That said, AdImpact doesn’t have full visibility into airings on every cable channel in every market in the country, hampering that estimate.
The White House defended the ad Sunday, pointing NBC News to a statement it had offered last week when it commented on the other ads released by the administration.
“These public service announcements are about reminding Americans to love their country and understand what makes it worth defending, at home, at our borders, and abroad. The ad is educational and unapologetically patriotic. We should be proud of our country,” a White House spokesperson said.
Another White House official pushed back on the line of questioning: “The PSAs are clearly not political. The president is not on the ballot, and the ads don’t have a call to action.”
The White House did not specifically respond to NBC News’ question about the ad’s being nearly identical to the 2024 Trump campaign ad.
A White House spokesperson also pointed to past examples of ads released by former administrations, including an ad by George W. Bush’s Department of Health and Human Services, a social media campaign by Barack Obama’s Environmental Protection Agency in 2014 and 2015 and an effort by Joe Biden’s administration encouraging Covid-19 vaccination.
The nonpartisan Government Accountability Office dinged the Bush and Obama ad campaigns — Bush’s for not properly disclosing the government was the source and Obama’s for violating “publicity or propaganda and anti-lobbying provisions.”
White House communications director Steven Cheung defended the recent pro-Trump ads Sunday on social media , writing, “Don’t let the Fake News get away with their lies about our epic Public Service Announcements that have been running on tv.”
CNN and The New York Times were first to report about the ad’s being almost identical to Trump’s 2024 campaign ad.
Spending taxpayer dollars on the ads has raised legal and ethical concerns and condemnation from both parties.
“This is the sort of government propaganda one might expect in North Korea, not the United States of America, and it is an egregious and utterly illegal misuse of Americans’ hard-earned tax dollars,” congressional Democratic appropriators wrote in a letter Friday addressed to White House chief of staff Susie Wiles.
The letter was signed by Sen. Patty Murray, D-Wash.; Sen. Jack Reed, D-R.I.; Rep. Rosa De Lauro, D-Conn.; and Rep. Steny Hoyer, D-Md.
Sen. John Kennedy, R-La., said Sunday in an interview with CBS that public officials should not “spend public money on private ads for themselves.”

In a Fox News Digital exclusive, Finnish President Alexander Stubb discusses efforts to end the war in Ukraine, pushes back on fears of a Russian attack on Finland and addresses growing military cooperation between Moscow and Tehran.
UNITED NATIONS — As Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy warns that Russia could take its war beyond Ukraine, Finnish President Alexander Stubb is striking a markedly calmer tone — saying Finland is prepared for Moscow and crediting President Donald Trump with pushing harder for a negotiated end to the war.
"I think we're certainly in a better place than we were before President Trump started," Stubb told Fox News Digital in an on-camera interview on the sidelines of the U.N. General Assembly in New York. "He's doubled down in the past year and a half to try to find a solution for peace with negotiators such as Steve Witkoff, Jared Kushner and many others."
Stubb, who has been closely involved in the diplomatic effort, said he and Norway’s prime minister have worked largely "in the back office," relaying information among Ukraine, the United States and European governments.
KUSHNER, WITKOFF SET FOR KYIV TALKS AFTER PUTIN MEETING IN US PUSH FOR PEACE
US President Donald Trump meets with Finnish President Alexander Stubb in the Oval Office of the White House in Washington, DC, on October 9, 2025. (Photo by Jim WATSON / AFP) (Photo by JIM WATSON/AFP via Getty Images) (Jim Watson/AFP via Getty Images)
"I think he's really working hard and hopefully we'll get a solution," Stubb said.
The interview came during an intense diplomatic week in New York focused heavily on the wars in Ukraine and the Middle East.
Trump and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy met in New York during UNGA week as Washington continued its effort to revive negotiations with Moscow. Zelenskyy said peace remained Ukraine's priority and thanked Trump for sending the two envoys to Kyiv after they had also held talks in Moscow.
Zelenskyy was asked by Fox News Digital after the meeting about the possibility that Russia could invade or attack another European country in the near future.
BATTLE-TESTED ZELENSKYY SOUNDS CHILLING ALARM ON WHERE PUTIN’S WAR COULD HEAD NEXT
Volodymyr Zelenskyy, Ukraine's president, left, and Alexander Stubb, Finland's president, right, during a news conference in Helsinki, Finland, on Wednesday, March 19, 2025. (Roni Rekomaa/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
"That's why the risk of offensive by drones, missiles or land operation is very high against other countries who are bordering Russia or Belarus ," Zelenskyy said.
The Ukrainian leader argued that Russian President Vladimir Putin , unable to achieve his military objectives in Ukraine, could seek to create instability elsewhere in Europe to pressure Western governments into reducing their support for Kyiv. He pointed to drone incursions and disruptions affecting several European countries, arguing that Moscow is already attempting to intimidate European societies and test their response.
Asked by Fox News Digital what European countries should do in response to the growing threat, Zelenskyy offered a direct answer.
"Respond. Always respond. It's not about the war. If you don't respond, Russians, they will go further," he said.
But Stubb struck a notably calmer tone when asked about Zelenskyy’s warnings that Russia could eventually attack other European countries, including Finland, which shares the longest border with Russia.
"As commander-in-chief in Finland, I sit on all the relevant information and I just don't see a factual basis for it," Stubb said.
RUSSIA'S SHADOW WAR IS PUTTING EUROPE ON EDGE AS GERMANY CONFRONTS A GROWING THREAT
Commander of the Finnish Army Lieutenant General Pasi Valimaki addresses Finnish conscript soldiers after a military exercise at Pori Brigade in Niinisalo, Finland, Dec. 9, 2025. (Anne Kauranen/Reuters)
That does not mean, he stressed, that Moscow has stopped targeting Europe.
Stubb distinguished between the "kinetic" war Russia is fighting in Ukraine and what he described as a broader "hybrid" campaign in Europe, pointing to cyberattacks, sabotage and damage to undersea cables in the Baltic Sea.
"We have to see this as a campaign," he said. "Russia tries to intimidate Europe, scare us and get into our heads."
His prescription was characteristically Finnish: "cool, calm and collected, take a sauna and a nice bath and deal with it."
Stubb said Finland, a country with a population of 5.6 million, can afford that attitude precisely because it has spent decades preparing for a potential threat from its eastern neighbor.
"We are calm because we are prepared," he said.
Finnish President Alexander Stubb answers questions during an exclusive Fox News Digital interview in New York City. (Brooke Curto / Fox News Digital)
He pointed to Finland’s mandatory military service, reserve force, artillery, long-range capabilities and extensive network of civilian shelters. The Finnish Defence Forces puts Finland’s wartime military strength at 280,000 personnel, with additional reservists available if needed.
That deterrent received another boost just days before Stubb traveled to New York. Finland is acquiring 64 F-35A fighter jets to replace its F/A-18 Hornet fleet under a procurement decision announced by the Finnish government.
The first two F-35s intended for operations inside Finland arrived at the Lapland Air Wing in Rovaniemi on Sept. 18, according to a Finnish Defence Forces press release.
"We have obligatory military service. I did mine, my son did his. We have women who do it voluntarily. We have over 60 F-18s. We just bought 64 F-35s, the two first of which arrived. We have long-range missiles, air, land and sea. We have the capability to mobilize 280,000 troops within days in a conflictual situation. On top of that, we have land mines. And we have the biggest artillery in Europe together with Poland… On top of that, we have civilian shelters for over 4.4 million people out of 5.6."
FINLAND'S PARLIAMENT VOTES TO LIFT DECADES-OLD BAN ON NUCLEAR WEAPONS IN HISTORIC NATO DEFENSE SHIFT
Security cameras overlook the Niirala Border Crossing Station along Finland's eastern border with Russia in Nov. 2023 after Finland closed the checkpoint amid heightened border security concerns. (Brooke Curto/Fox News Digital)
"We don't have them because we're worried about Sweden," Stubb joked of Finland’s military capabilities. "We have them because we see a security threat coming from Russia."
He said that level of preparedness, combined with Finland’s NATO membership, makes a direct Russian attack unlikely. Finland became NATO's 31st member on April 4, 2023, after abandoning its longstanding military non-alignment following Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
"We feel that we're very prepared, and that gives us a strong enough … deterrent that we don't believe that Russia is going to test a country like Finland," Stubb said. "And of course the icing on the cake is that we are now security providers in the Alliance NATO."
Stubb also used his Sept. 22 address to the U.N. General Assembly to advocate for continued support for Kyiv, calling the "Coalition of the Willing" supporting Ukraine "particularly close to my heart." He said the coalition was working toward a "just and lasting peace in Ukraine in accordance with the U.N. Charter."
Stubb made additional news on Ukraine during UNGA week, when he urged SpaceX owner Elon Musk to extend Starlink coverage so Ukrainian forces could use the satellite network in areas containing Russian ballistic missile launchers , including inside Russia. He argued that doing so could help Ukraine target launchers firing missiles at Ukrainian cities.
Yet Ukraine was only one piece of what Stubb described as an increasingly interconnected global security crisis.

The Open Agent Safety Platform is designed to enforce AI boundaries.
The Open Agent Safety Platform is designed to enforce AI boundaries.
Nvidia is launching a new safety platform designed to contain and monitor AI agents, a move that comes in response to a wave of rogue hacking incidents , as reported earlier by Reuters . In an announcement on Monday , Nvidia says its new Open Agent Safety Platform can quarantine agents that attempt to escape their boundaries within “milliseconds.”
The platform uses Nvidia’s OpenShell open-source software, which runs on the company’s Vera AI CPU . Users can choose the information an AI agent can access, and OpenShell checks these restrictions before and during a task, according to Nvidia . It also includes Nvidia’s Sentry technology on a separate chip to continuously monitor agents and enforce boundaries.
During an interview with CNBC , Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang emphasized the importance of giving AI agents access to only the information they need to do their job. “In order for you to deliver that agentic system in a safe way, you have to make sure that the sandbox around it… all of those systems are designed in a way that keeps the agent with minimal rights,” Huang said.
Concerns about AI safety have risen in recent weeks , as OpenAI , Anthropic , and Google have all revealed incidents where their AI models went outside their testing environments and hacked other companies. Several major tech companies are backing Nvidia’s Open Agent Safety Platform, including Anthropic, Microsoft, and SpaceX.

Gold and silver prices slipped sharply on Monday, as rising global bond yields cooled investor appetite for non-interest-bearing assets, like precious metals. The sell-off also dragged major mining stocks lower in premarket trading.
Gold futures slumped 3.34% to $4,176.80, while spot gold prices were off by 3.27% at $4,145.88 around 5:40 a.m. E.T.
Silver, meanwhile, fell even further. Silver futures were last seen 5.1% lower at $61.52 per troy ounce, while spot silver had shed 4.92% to $61.11.
U.S.-listed shares of global gold and silver miners dropped in premarket trading on the back of the retreat.
Sibanye Stillwater , a major gold producer which is also active in platinum and palladium markets, was 7.92% lower ahead of Monday's market open, while Harmony Gold Mining slumped 7.49%. Newmont Corporation was down 4.72% in premarket trading.
Among silver miners, Silvercorp Metals was down 7.13%, Endeavour Silver shed 5.86%, and Hecla Mining dipped 5.55%.
The downward moves come as investors continue to monitor inflationary pressures and the likelihood of further interest rate hikes from the Federal Reserve against a backdrop of surging government bond yields .
"If hikes bring inflation under control, gold faces sustained pressure," Max Baecker, president of American Hartford Gold, said in a note Friday. "If inflation sticks or economic stress builds, demand for gold as a diversifier holds."
Baecker added that rates are "just one piece of the gold story," noting how global central banks purchased a record 289 metric tons in the second quarter, which he sees as a longer-term reserve strategy separate from Fed rate decisions.

articles.title_zh: China, US agree to tariff cuts on $60 billion of goods including agriculture, household items
articles.content_orig:
BEIJING — The U.S. and China are planning to reduce tariffs on $30 billion worth of goods from each country, according to government announcements from both sides Monday.
The detailed lists includes mostly imports of toys, sports equipment and Christmas decorations by the U.S., while American agricultural products accounted for much of the far longer list of imports by China.
Washington has sought to reduce its record trade deficit with Beijing, as the Asian country exports far more to the U.S. than it imports. U.S. goods trade deficit with China was more than $202 billion last year.
"If we see the tariff cuts actually implemented before the holiday season, it could provide a welcome boost to U.S. consumption and to retailers," said Jacob Cooke, CEO at WPIC.
Cooke, whose company primarily helps U.S. brands sell in China, said that Beijing's import list includes fast-growing categories such as hair care and packaged pet food, where Chinese brands are highly competitive against U.S. offerings. "Every percentage point counts for price competitiveness and preserving margin."
However, it was not immediately clear when lower tariffs would take effect, and by how much the duties would go down. The U.S. and China last year slapped import tariffs effectively of over 40% and more than 30%, respectively, on each other.
The two countries limited further tariff increases after a one-year truce reached last fall. Last week, U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said negotiators agreed to extend that truce to January.
Monday's announcement followed U.S. President Donald Trump's summit with Chinese President Xi Jinping in Washington, D.C., last week. The two sides said the highly anticipated U.S.-China "Board of Trade" would consist of officials from both governments, and would meet at least once a quarter , with the top officials meeting "whenever necessary."
Lower tariffs could substantially boost trade, especially for highly competitive Chinese companies. Home goods seller Ryan Zhao, director of Jiangsu Green Willow Textile, expects sales in the second half of the year to grow by 30% from a year ago if tariff cuts are implemented.

articles.title_orig: Base jumper dies in Utah after wingsuit fails in remote mountainous region
articles.title_zh: Base jumper dies in Utah after wingsuit fails in remote mountainous region
articles.content_orig:
A 27-year-old BASE jumper died Sunday after his wingsuit failed when he launched from a 700-foot perch in Utah, authorities said.
The man, whose identity was withheld until his family could be notified, fatally plunged from a mountainous area of Hyrum, Utah, east of Millville Canyon and east of the small city of Millville, Cache County Chief Sheriff’s Deputy Doyle Peck said.
Search-and-rescue crews were called to Leetham’s Hollow, an area of canyon walls and cliffs not unlike the Grand Canyon’s, at 9:10 a.m. Sunday and declared the man dead at the scene, Peck said in a statement.
“On today’s jump, something went wrong and he did not have enough lift with his wingsuit,” Peck said. “He impacted the ground at a high rate of speed resulting in his death.”
The man was “experienced in this type of activity” and was part of a group of as many as 10 people who appeared to be engaged in wingsuit-aided BASE jumping, according to Peck.
The area, about 45 miles north of Ogden, is popular with BASE jumpers, he said.
A medical transport helicopter sent to help with the initial search transported the man’s body, Peck said.
Before Sunday, 541 deaths around the world since 1981 had been logged by the BASE Fatality List , maintained by an online community for the sport. This year, 15 such deaths have been reported globally, according to the list.
In June, two BASE jumpers died in a separate accident in Utah . One of them, Andy Lewis, performed onstage with Madonna at the 2012 Super Bowl.
Photographer Carl Boenish helped coin BASE as a description of the sport’s adrenaline-inspiring launch points (buildings, antennas, spans, earth) in 1978, when he videotaped early jumps from Yosemite National Park’s El Capitan rock formation.

articles.title_zh: Russian strikes on Ukraine kill at least 7, including woman at Kyiv's National Academy of Sciences
articles.content_orig:
Three others wounded as jet-powered drones increasingly target Ukraine’s capital, with medical centre also hit
Europe live – latest updates
A Russian drone hit the National Academy of Sciences in central Kyiv on Monday, killing at least one person, in the latest daytime attack on Ukraine’s capital.
Flames tore through the historic building as people clambered out of first- and second-floor windows to escape, in dramatic scenes increasingly familiar in the heavily bombarded city.
At least one person was killed and three others were wounded, according to Kyiv’s mayor, Vitali Klitschko , who said the injured had been taken to hospital.
The 19th-century building stands close to the German embassy, the National Opera, St Volodymyr’s Cathedral and several government buildings.
Anatoliy Zagorodny, the president of the national academy, said the blast struck while many staff members were inside. Standing outside the burning building, he said he did not know why Russia had targeted a leading centre of scientific research.
“We are not connected with the military. This is an attack on science. It is terrorism,” he said. He feared some of his colleagues could still be trapped inside the academy.
While the sciences building is a civilian scientific institution, it has longstanding ties to Ukraine’s defence sector. Among those injured in Monday’s strike was Volodymyr Horbulin, the academy’s first vice-president and a former high-ranking security official.
Another Russian drone struck a nearby private medical centre, killing at least one person.
Russian strikes over the past week involving missiles and increasingly sophisticated jet-powered drones have hit apartment blocks, offices, warehouses and datacentres across the capital, killing and wounding civilians almost daily and giving Kyiv an increasingly frontline feel as it faces some of its most sustained bombardment since the early stages of Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022.
The drone and missile campaign is designed to grind down public resilience and damage the economy. Monday’s double strike is likely to raise fresh concerns over Ukraine’s ability to protect even the most heavily guarded parts of the capital.
The newer jet-powered drones fly faster and are harder to intercept than the older Shahed or Geran-2 models that were the backbone of Moscow’s air campaign. Ukraine is racing to develop and manufacture interceptors capable of bringing them down.
Moscow has also changed its tactics, launching more attacks in daylight hours so that residents in major cities have to spend more of the day under air raid alerts.
after newsletter promotion
Buildings hit during daytime strikes are often occupied because many Ukrainians work through drone alerts rather than spend hours in shelters.
Meanwhile, a Russian jet-powered drone struck western Ukraine near the border crossing with Poland, prompting Warsaw to issue an alert warning of a possible air attack and urging residents in the eastern Lublin region to seek shelter.
Russian forces have increasingly targeted Ukrainian border crossings with Poland and Moldova, leading Kyiv to consider relocating joint customs checkpoints to the territory of neighbouring countries. “It’s again a threat very close to our border,” said Lt Col Jacek Goryszewski, speaking to Poland’s broadcaster TVN24.
Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy , called on western countries to intensify their pressure on Russia. “Every Russian terrorist attack is a loss of life that could have been prevented if pressure on Russia had finally become total,” he wrote on X on Monday. “The world must understand that terrorists will go further if they are not stopped here, in Ukraine. And we cannot turn a blind eye to such brutal strikes.”
Russia has signalled that its attacks on Ukraine could intensify, and US-brokered efforts to end the war show little sign of progress.
“Ukraine will have to pay a price for the actions that have taken place in recent months,” the Kremlin spokesperson, Dmitry Peskov, told reporters on Monday, referring to Ukrainian strikes deep inside Russian territory. “That is happening right now.”

(Kitco News) – China’s 2026 gold imports could be double those of last year, and will set the high-water mark for the 2020s to date, while silver prices are approaching a key test that could determine the gray metal’s near-term direction, according to precious metals analysts at Heraeus.
In their latest update, the analysts noted that China’s gold imports have already exceeded 2025 totals in 2026. “China imported 142 tonnes of gold in August, taking imports during the first eight months of the year to 1,141 tonnes, 72% higher than the 663 tonnes imported over the same period last year, and higher than the 940 tonnes imported during the whole of 2025,” they wrote. “The strong inflows come despite historically high gold prices and reflect continued investment demand, while Chinese jewellery demand remains comparatively weak. These non-monetary imports are separate from purchases by the People’s Bank of China, which added a further 20 tonnes to its official reserves in August.”
“If Chinese gold imports maintain this pace through the rest of 2026, they will total ~1,700 tonnes, which would represent the highest amount this decade.”
Australia’s gold mine production continued to rise in fiscal year 2025-26 as historically high prices continue to support the mining sector. “Australia produced 303 tonnes of gold up to the end of its financial year in June, broadly in line with its long-run production rate of around 300 tonnes p.a.,” the analysts said. “Output improved at most operations during the June quarter, while several smaller producers also began production. The 303 tonnes produced in Australia account for around 8% of total mined gold supply, which was 3,822 tonnes in 2025.”
Heraeus said Indonesia is proposing a scheme to incentivize privately held gold stocks to be invested into the formal financial system. “The government estimates that households hold around 1,800 tonnes of gold outside formal investment channels and has asked state-owned institutions to encourage around 20% of this metal, equivalent to roughly 360 tonnes, into bullion-banking and financial products,” they wrote. “The initiative is aimed at turning privately held metal into deposits, collateral and other financial assets, deepening the domestic bullion market and potentially increasing the amount of household wealth circulating through the financial system.”
The analysts also warned that India’s weak monsoon will likely depress rural gold demand during this year’s festival and wedding season – and rural demand represents over 50% of the country’s total bullion consumption. “Monsoon rainfall was around 15% below its long-run average by late September, presenting a downside risk to gold demand due to the potential of lower crop yields to impact rural incomes,” they said. “Historical analysis by the World Gold Council suggests that a 1% increase in rainfall relative to the average is associated with a 0.2% increase in gold demand, implying that this year’s rainfall deficit could represent a modest headwind. Indian gold demand totalled 768 tonnes in 2025, roughly 15% of global demand.”
Spot gold was continuing to test session lows early in the North American session, and last traded at $4,142.30 for a loss of 3.33% on the daily chart.
Turning to silver, Heraeus analysts noted that the renewed strength of the U.S. dollar has driven silver prices to a key inflection point.
“Silver prices dropped below $65/oz last week as the dollar index rose back above 101.0, towards its yearly highs,” they noted. “This leaves silver at an important level. A renewed rally back towards $70/oz despite a rising dollar, a hawkish Federal Reserve and rising bond yields could signal a confirmation of a potential bottoming process. However, if silver falls back below $60/oz, this could be the sign of a continuation of the bearish downtrend, marked by lower highs and lower lows, in which silver has been stuck since its late January peak.”
The analysts wrote that the 10-year Treasury yield’s rise to 5.22% and the 10-year Treasury Inflation-Protected Security (TIPS) real yield hitting 2.8% indicates that the Federal Reserve’s 25 basis point rate hike in September was not enough to reassure markets.
“The rise in real yields alongside nominal yields is particularly significant for precious metals, indicating that the sell-off in Treasuries has not been driven solely by higher inflation expectations, but also by investors demanding a higher inflation-adjusted return, consistent with the anticipation that monetary policy could remain tighter for longer,” they said. “This comes as Brent crude remains around $100/bbl, and despite renewed talks between the US and Iran, a deal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz does not appear imminent.”
And Indian silver imports spiked higher in August after several months of weak inflows. “India imported 15.5 moz of silver in August, the first time since February that monthly imports have topped 10 moz and 36% higher than the 11.4 moz imported in August 2025,” the analysts wrote. “Despite the strong monthly recovery, imports remain weak for the year as a whole, with an estimated 75.6 moz imported during January-August, 24% less than the 99.1 moz imported over the same period last year.”
“The rebound follows several months of unusually low imports after the licensing requirements introduced in May complicated the import process and high silver prices reduced demand, they said. “The upswing in August suggests that physical inflows are beginning to normalise, although year-to-date imports remain well below last year’s levels.”
Silver prices were also trading just above their earlier session lows on Monday morning after dipping below $61 per ounce around 5 am ET.
Spot silver last traded at $61.302 per ounce for a loss of 4.67% on the daily chart.

articles.title_zh: Benjamin Satterley, pro wrestler known as "Pac," dies at age 40
articles.content_orig:
Benjamin Satterley, an English-born wrestler known for high-flying moves that delighted fans worldwide, has died. He was 40.
The death of Satterley, who was known as "Pac," was announced late Sunday on All Elite Wrestling's website . The website did not list a cause of death.
"Our condolences go out to Satterley's family, friends and fans," All Elite Wrestling wrote on social media.
All Elite Wrestling is saddened to announce the passing of Benjamin Satterley, aka Pac. A native of Newcastle upon Tyne, England, Satterley began his wrestling career in 2004 and went on to perform for wrestling organizations all over the world, captivating fans with innovative… pic.twitter.com/uqzO371t2V
Satterley, who was from Newcastle upon Tyne, began his wrestling career in 2004 and signed in 2019 with All Elite Wrestling, where he held multiple championships.
He competed and lost to Andrade El Ídolo on Saturday in Chicago in the AEW National Championship.
Satterley began his wrestling training when he was 18 after developing an interest for the sport through his aunt, who was a fan of the WWF, according to MN2S, his booking agency.
He quickly rose to prominence, earning nicknames like "The Super Superman" and "The Man That Gravity Forgot." He began his international journey in 2007 and wrestled under the name of Adrian Neville from 2012 to 2018.
After signing with AEW, he became the inaugural AEW International Champion and a two-time AEW World Trios Champion.
Tributes for Satterley have poured in.
"The greatest export from our country. Also the greatest human being," fellow wrestler Will Ospreay wrote on X . "Honored to have shared the ring with you so many times. You truly are such a hero to myself and many others."
"The best lad… We love you," wrote fellow wrestler Kevin Owens along with photos of him and Pac.
Wrestler Alexa Bliss wrote on social media: "I cannot believe this. RIP PAC 💔"

BEIJING -- The China Open begins a two-event WTA 1000 stretch on the Asian Swing, with main-draw play starting Wednesday, Sept. 30.
World No. 1 Elena Rybakina is the top seed, followed by Aryna Sabalenka, Coco Gauff and Mirra Andreeva. Each is seeded to lead a quarter of the draw.
Gauff, the 2024 champion, is one of three former Beijing winners in the field, alongside Iga Swiatek (2023) and Naomi Osaka (2019).
Here is a quarter-by-quarter breakdown of the draw, including first-round matches to watch and potential quarterfinal matchups.
To see the full draw, click here .
Note: Qualifying will finish on Tuesday, Sept. 29. More first-round matches will be confirmed then.
[WC] Zheng Qinwen vs. Qualifier (TBD): While Zheng's opponent will be determined after qualifying, seeing how Zheng plans to continue the stretch of strong play from the US Open will be something to watch. After a first-round qualifying exit in Toronto, Zheng went back to the practice court in an intense training program that fueled her US Open quarterfinal run.

articles.title_zh: Google is officially killing Gemini Gems
articles.content_orig:

If you’re an avid Gemini user and have created a bunch of Gemini Gems tailored to your needs and preferences, we have good and bad news for you today. After months of hearing about Google’s plans to sunset Gems in favor of Skills, and finding code in the Google app hinting at the same, Google has finally made an official announcement.
Opening the Gems manager in Gemini now shows a banner announcing Google’s plan to end Gems support starting November 17. That’s the bad news, but there’s a bit of good news as well, though with some confusion that Google has yet to clear up.
According to the banner, Google will start “migrating your Gems to Skills” starting November 17, and you will be able to use your Gems until they are migrated. Theoretically, this could take longer than a few days, which makes it seem as though your Gems might last for a few extra days past that mid-November deadline. You will also be able to continue using your Gems in the form of Skills once they are migrated, so you won’t lose all the work you put into them.
The confusing part lies in Google’s plans for giving users access to Skills. While Gems are available to all users, including those with free accounts, Skills are (as of right now) only available to those with a Google AI Pro or Ultra subscription and access to Gemini Spark .
If Google migrates Gems to Skills, is it also planning to let users with free accounts create and access Skills in Gemini? That would be the logical conclusion. However, the “Learn More” button in the banner currently leads to a Google Support page that doesn’t exist. That page will likely include a more detailed explanation of Google’s plans regarding Skills access for free accounts.
For now, you should prepare for Gems to go away in a little over a month’s time. Here’s hoping Google won’t just hang free users out to dry, migrating their Gems to Skills and forcing them to upgrade to a Google AI Pro or Ultra account to access those Skills.
We have reached out to Google for comment and will update this story when we hear back.

articles.title_orig: Turtle Beach Afterglow Review: A Switch 2 Controller With The Full RGB Treatment
articles.title_zh: Turtle Beach Afterglow Review: A Switch 2 Controller With The Full RGB Treatment
articles.content_orig:
This is for the gamer who wants RGB everything.
Maybe I'm feeding into a stereotype, perhaps it makes me a basic gamer, but dang it — I love RGB lighting. I want it in my keyboard, mouse, PC case, headphones, game consoles and behind every screen in the house, layering a subtle sci-fi glow over my entire space. At night, I want to fall asleep beneath shifting rainbow galaxies. I want to cradle an LED prism in my hands. Even better if it can control my video games, too.
You see where this is heading. The Turtle Beach Afterglow Wireless Controller for Nintendo Switch 2 is a transparent gamepad with variable RGB light settings, and it looks like a handheld cosmic gemstone. On top of its aesthetic allure, the Switch 2 Afterglow is a responsive, low-latency controller with a wireless range of up to 30 feet and ultra-precise TMR thumbsticks, which provide a long-term drift-free guarantee. In action, the gamepad is nicely reactive and comfortable to hold for hours on end, with hard, clicky face buttons, cushioned trigger pulls and mappable rear paddles that can be super satisfying fidget toys when not actually in use. The back buttons function independently, but they're connected by a matte black bridge, adding a secondary sensory pop beneath the opposite fingertip with each press.
Aside from an additional strip of shiny black between the triggers and shoulder buttons, housing the USB-C charging point and bluetooth connection, the controller chassis is clear plastic. Even the grips aren't textured, lending the whole thing a crisp, crystalline look whether the lights are off or on. Switch 2 controllers tend to be rather small and light, a fact that I personally love, and the Afterglow fits this description. It's similar in size and weight to the official Switch 2 Pro Controller, the console's reigning standard. Of course, the Pro costs $90 while the Afterglow costs $65 and is often on sale for far less.
The lack of texture on the grips hasn't been an issue for me, even after playing Resident Evil Requiem for a few hours to really test out the sweat factor. The Switch 2 Afterglow is comfortable to hold for long periods of time; it's never unexpectedly slipped out of my hands or threatened to throw off my zombie-hunting game in first- or third-person. It also handles Hello Kitty Island Adventure like a champ.
The Afterglow's buttons are black with symbols and letters etched into the faces, which brings me to a gripe I have with nearly all Switch 2 controllers, including Nintendo's own: The minus, plus, home and other small face buttons are nearly impossible to read. This fact is particularly frustrating when you're using a gamepad for the first time and getting used to its layout. The Switch 2 Afterglow, for instance, has a dedicated GameChat button in the center of the array, plus and minus buttons above that, and Home and Capture above those. I accidentally took a handful of random screenshots while reaching blindly for the minus button to open the map in Requiem , and I was never quite able to shake off the incorrect muscle memory. I'd love if the icons were highlighted to make the small buttons more readable at a quick glance.
The Switch 2 Afterglow has motion-control capabilities but it doesn't feature any haptics, so there's no rumble here. Its analog sticks use top-of-the-line TMR technology, which promises long-term accuracy without the risk of drift, and they make a nice clacky sound when they hit the sides of their enclosures. The tops of the Afterglow thumbsticks have fairly high, defined edges with a textured divot for your thumbpad, and they're easy to press in even at an angle.
In the box, the Afterglow comes with a 1-meter charging cable and it boasts a battery life of 40 hours — but that's with no RGBs ( why? ). Turtle Beach's Switch 2 controllers generally get 12 hours of playtime with RGB lighting effects on, and that's likely to be the case here, too. This particular model isn't able to wake up the Switch 2, but it connects seamlessly to the console once it's on.
Now, let's talk about those RGBs.
The Afterglow has four lighting modes, adjustable by holding the small circle beneath the right thumbstick, and then pressing the L or R bumpers. The LED settings are as follows: On and steady, pulsing in one color, cycling through all colors, and reactive to stick movement. You're able to set the colors and adjust brightness on the fly as well, and it's all super simple. The lights are vibrant and fill the entirety of the gamepad with a clean radiance. The RGB instructions live right here , for quick reference.
My favorite setting is the input-responsive one, where the controller lights up in a specific color depending on which direction the analog stick travels, generating a rainbow light show as you play. But truly, the Afterglow makes me smile no matter which mode it's set to. Even off, it's a slick-looking gamepad.
But again, I'm a sucker for this stuff. I love transparent gadgets with their motherboards and mechanical guts exposed, and I adore RGB lights. The Turtle Beach Afterglow for Switch 2 combines these styles in a delicious way, and it happens to be a precise and responsive gamepad, to boot. I'm happy to have one, here in my crystal kingdom.

articles.content_orig:
Manufacturing capacity is moving overseas but China, as a global hub for innovation and development, remains the ‘industrial brain’
The global electronics industry is entering a structural transition. For over two decades, China served as the dominant manufacturing centre, with an unmatched concentration of suppliers, skilled labour, infrastructure, logistics and engineering capabilities. That concentration is being diluted. But interpreting this as the decline of Chinese manufacturing would be a mistake.
According to the Boston Consulting Group (BCG), since 2017, the share of electronics manufacturers from China – Taiwan, Hong Kong and the mainland – with overseas production has risen to 56 per cent from 12 per cent. BCG based its analysis on 942 publicly traded companies with annual revenues above US$500 million, including 314 headquartered in China. This transformation is remarkable.

Giants pass rusher Brian Burns’ season appears to be over.
Burns is believed to have suffered a torn ACL on Sunday, according to Adam Schefter.
The injury is a devastating one for the Giants’ defense. Burns has started every game for the Giants since they traded for him in 2024, and last year he had a career-high 16.5 sacks.
Burns is in the third year of the five-year, $141 million contract he signed in 2024.
Until late last week, Burns was expected to miss Sunday’s game because of the low ankle sprain he suffered the week before. Instead he played, and played what turned out to be his last game of the season.

U.K. police say they arrested multiple suspects for offenses under the "Explosives Act" near a U.S. airbase in southwest England on Sunday.
Gloucestershire Police say the arrests took place just two miles from RAF Fairford, which hosts U.S. Air Force assets. The U.S. has recently used the base in operations relating to the war in Iran.
"A number of properties are currently being evacuated in the Whelford area following the declaration of a major incident," Gloucestershire Police said in a statement. "It follows the arrest of several men on suspicion of offenses under the explosives act."

"The Army's specialist explosive ordnance disposal team are currently examining a number of vehicles," police added.
President Donald Trump responded to news of the arrests while talking to the press later Sunday.
"The arrest in the UK was fantastic. Working with Britain. It was an amazing job. We had them under investigation," Trump said of the suspects. "They, they were looking to do big damage to our fort and working with the British worked out great."
A reporter then asked if the suspects were migrants, and Trump demurred.
"It may have been Scotland Yard. I don't know that we worked with a lot of them. We had them under review for a long time and we got them," Trump said.
Authorities did not name the suspects or detail exactly how many were arrested.
British Defense Secretary Wes Streeting wrote on X that the situation is "being dealt with."

"I know today's incident near RAF Fairford will be deeply concerning for local residents and for many people following developments across the country. My thanks go to Gloucestershire Police, Counter Terrorism Policing, our Armed Forces and all those working to keep the public safe," he said.
"The safety and security of the public is our first priority, and I want people to know that we will always take every step necessary to protect our communities and keep our country safe. The investigation remains ongoing, and I would urge people not to speculate while the authorities establish the full facts," he added.

The British shutdown came weeks after hackers struck more than 30 community water systems in Minnesota , accessing technology used to remotely monitor and control pumps and other equipment.
